name: Bruising
preview_text: A bruise’s color, pain quality, and how easily it appears reveal distinct TCM patterns - and treating the root cause can speed healing and reduce future bruising.
synonyms: ["Bruise", "Bruises", "Skin Discoloration From Trauma", "Tendency to bruise easily", "Ecchymosis", "Purplish discolouration or bruising of the skin", "Contusion", "Contusions", "Skin Contusions", "Easy Bruising or Subcutaneous Bleeding", "Easy bruising or petechiae", "Easy bruising or subcutaneous purple spots", "Easy bruising or subcutaneous purpura", "Petechiae and easy bruising of undetermined cause"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, a bruise (ecchymosis) occurs when small blood vessels break and leak blood into the tissues beneath the skin, usually after a bump or injury. The trapped blood causes the characteristic blue, purple, or black discoloration that changes color as it heals. Most bruises are harmless and fade on their own within two weeks.
When bruising happens very easily or without any remembered injury, doctors may investigate for bleeding disorders, vitamin deficiencies, or medications that thin the blood. The standard approach focuses on symptom relief and ruling out serious underlying conditions.
conventional_treatments: For a fresh bruise, the usual advice is rest, ice, compression, and elevation (RICE) to limit swelling. Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen can help with discomfort, though NSAIDs like ibuprofen are sometimes avoided because they can increase bleeding. For people who bruise easily, treatment targets the underlying cause - adjusting medications, supplementing vitamin C or K, or addressing a bleeding disorder.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, a bruise is understood as Blood Stagnation (瘀血, yū xuè) - blood that has leaked out of the vessels and become stuck. The Liver is the organ most responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and Blood throughout the body, while the Spleen holds blood inside the vessels. When Qi moves strongly, blood circulates; when it stagnates, blood pools and a bruise forms.
The type of bruise tells a story. A dark, fixed bruise with stabbing pain after a direct blow is classic Blood Stagnation. A bruise that comes with stress, a distending ache, and shifting pain points to Qi and Blood Stagnation - the Liver’s Qi is stuck and can’t move the blood. If bruises appear from the lightest touch and look pale, the root is often Qi and Blood Deficiency or Spleen Qi failing to hold blood in the vessels.
External factors also matter. Cold constricts the channels and slows circulation, causing stiff, aching bruises that feel worse in cold weather. Heat can turn a bruise red, hot, and swollen, indicating inflammation and possible infection. This is why the same Western symptom - a bruise - can have six different TCM patterns, each requiring a different treatment strategy.
classical_quote: 「人有所堕坠，恶血留内，腹中满胀，不得前后，先饮利药。」
classical_translation: "When a person falls or is injured by a heavy blow, stagnant blood remains inside, causing abdominal fullness and distension, and difficulty with urination and defecation. First, administer a purgative to remove the stagnant blood."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing Ling Shu (The Spiritual Pivot)  ,  Chapter 10, Jing Mai (The Meridians) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening carefully to how the bruise feels and how it came about. The quality of the pain - whether it is fixed, stabbing, or distending - and the color of the discoloration are the first big clues. They also ask about your energy level, any emotional stress, and whether the area feels hot or cold to the touch. These details start to separate one pattern from another.
When the pain is fixed and piercing, and the bruise is a deep, dark purple that stays in one place, the picture points to pure Blood Stagnation. The tongue often looks dark or purplish with tiny stagnant spots, and the pulse feels choppy or wiry. This pattern is very common after a direct blow, where blood has simply pooled and congealed in the local tissues.
If the bruise comes with a distending, moving pain and you feel emotionally tense or stressed, the diagnosis leans toward Qi and Blood Stagnation. Here the bruise may shift or feel more like a dull ache that spreads. The tongue may be slightly dusky, and the pulse is often wiry, reflecting the stuck Qi that is failing to move the blood smoothly.
When bruising happens easily or heals slowly, the practitioner looks for signs of deficiency. Pale bruises, general fatigue, a pale tongue with a thin white coat, and a weak or thready pulse suggest the body lacks enough Qi and Blood to repair itself. This could be Qi Deficiency causing Blood Stagnation, where the engine is too weak to push blood along, or a broader Qi and Blood Deficiency that leaves tissues undernourished and fragile.

patterns.why_this_happens: When a bump or injury damages the small vessels, blood leaks into the tissues and gets stuck. Because it's no longer moving, it becomes stagnant and appears as a dark purple or bluish bruise. This stagnant blood presses on nerves and blocks the free flow of Qi, producing the characteristic fixed, stabbing pain that worsens at night and with pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots and distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) like a knife scraping bamboo, or wiry (弦 xián) if Qi stagnation is present.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold causes contraction and freezing of Blood, which directly worsens stagnation and pain, so warmth and gentle movement help dissolve stasis. Rest allows the body to repair, but too much inactivity causes Qi to stagnate further, preventing the bruise from clearing. Stress and frustration knot the Liver Qi, which in turn worsens Blood stasis, so keeping calm and moving gently breaks the cycle of stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold and raw foods, which can congeal Blood and worsen stasis. Eat moderate amounts of Blood-moving foods like turmeric, dark cherries, eggplant, and dark leafy greens. Gentle daily movement such as walking or stretching helps keep Qi and Blood flowing, but avoid heavy impact on the bruised area. Apply a warm compress briefly after the first 24 hours to encourage circulation and speed healing.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When emotional stress, frustration, or trauma disrupts the smooth flow of Qi, the Liver’s ability to move blood is compromised. Stagnant Qi fails to propel blood, causing it to pool and form bruises. The result is a bruise that often feels distended or pressure-like, and its pain may shift rather than staying fixed.
Because the root is a Qi blockage, the bruising can appear or worsen after emotional upset, and it is frequently accompanied by chest tightness, rib-side discomfort, and irritability.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended and tortuous sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (xian) and choppy (se) - taut like a guitar string, yet rough and uneven.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly knots Liver Qi, the very engine that moves blood; when Qi stalls, blood stagnates and bruises form. Inactivity and cold both slow circulation, while heavy, greasy foods create dampness that further obstructs flow. Gentle movement, warmth, and relaxation all encourage Qi to unblock and blood to circulate, allowing the stasis to resolve and the bruise to heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the body gently moving with walking, stretching, or tai chi to encourage Qi flow. Use warming spices like turmeric and ginger in cooking, and avoid cold, raw foods that can congeal blood. Prioritize stress management - deep breathing, meditation, or talking things out - to prevent Liver Qi from knotting up.

patterns.why_this_happens: When both Qi and Blood are deficient, the body lacks the vital force to keep blood sealed inside the vessels. Minor bumps that would barely leave a mark in a healthy person can break fragile capillaries, causing pale bruises that appear easily. Because Qi is too weak to move stagnant blood and Blood is too scanty to repair the tissue, the bruises linger and heal much more slowly than normal.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks on the sides, with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak (细弱 xì ruò), lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overexertion and stress drain Qi, leaving even less force to keep blood in the vessels and repair damaged tissue. Cold and raw foods damage Spleen Yang, impairing the production of new Qi and Blood. Rest and warmth conserve and slowly rebuild these vital substances, while gentle movement circulates Qi without depleting it, helping the body clear old bruises and prevent new ones.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize warm, cooked meals like soups and stews that are easy to digest and rich in nourishment - bone broth, dark leafy greens, small amounts of red meat if tolerated, and a few dates or goji berries. Avoid cold, raw foods and iced drinks which weaken the Spleen's ability to produce Qi and Blood. Gentle daily movement like walking or stretching helps circulation without draining your reserves, and getting enough deep rest is non-negotiable.

patterns.why_this_happens: When a bruise becomes infected or the body already carries internal heat toxins, the trapped blood turns from simple stagnation into a hot, inflammatory state. The heat accelerates tissue damage, making the bruise red, swollen, and intensely painful. This combination of static blood and heat creates a vicious cycle - the stuck blood generates more heat, and the heat further thickens and congeals the blood.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: reddish-purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, and a thin dry yellow coating. Pulse: choppy (涩, sè) and rapid (数, shuò), often wiry (弦, xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat is the driving force behind this pattern - it inflames the bruise, thickens the blood, and intensifies pain. Anything that adds heat to the body, like spicy food, alcohol, or hot environments, will worsen the condition. Cooling measures, both external and dietary, counteract that heat, calm the inflammation, and help the stagnant blood disperse. Rest prevents further internal heat generation from activity and gives the body space to clear the stasis.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods that generate internal heat. Keep the bruised area clean and protected from further trauma or infection. A cool (not freezing) compress can soothe acute heat and swelling. Eat more cooling, blood-moving foods like cucumber, celery, and a little black fungus.

patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the bruised area warm with clothing or a heating pad. Avoid cold exposure and drafts. Eat warming foods like ginger, cinnamon, lamb and cooked vegetables, and steer clear of raw, chilled foods and icy drinks. Gentle movement that warms the joints without strain helps keep blood flowing.

faqs.question: Can TCM help a bruise heal faster?
faqs.answer: Yes. Herbs like Dang Gui and Hong Hua move blood and reduce swelling, while acupuncture points such as Xuehai SP-10 and Sanyinjiao SP-6 invigorate circulation. For a fresh bruise, apply a cool compress for the first 24 hours, then switch to warm applications and gentle movement to encourage blood flow. Many people find the discoloration fades noticeably quicker than it would on its own.

faqs.question: I bruise easily without any injury. What does TCM say?
faqs.answer: This is often a sign that your Spleen Qi is too weak to keep blood inside the vessels, or that your overall Qi and Blood are deficient. When the body lacks the vital force to seal the capillaries, even minor bumps cause leaks. A TCM practitioner will look at your tongue, pulse, and energy level to pinpoint the pattern and prescribe herbs like Huang Qi and Dang Gui to strengthen you from within.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with blood-thinning medications?
faqs.answer: Caution is essential. Many blood-moving herbs - including Dang Gui, Chuan Xiong, and Hong Hua - can increase bleeding risk when taken alongside warfarin, aspirin, or clopidogrel. Always tell both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about every medication and supplement you use. They can adjust formulas or monitor you more closely to keep you safe.

faqs.question: How long until I see results from TCM for bruising?
faqs.answer: Acute bruises often improve within a week. Chronic easy bruising or old bruises that won’t fade may take 4-12 weeks of consistent treatment, because the goal is to rebuild your Qi and Blood rather than just clear one mark. Your practitioner will track changes in your energy, tongue, and pulse to gauge progress.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with an old bruise that still hurts?
faqs.answer: Yes. Stagnant blood that has been sitting for weeks or months can create a persistent ache. Acupuncture needles placed locally and at distal points like Taichong LR-3 and Hegu LI-4 help break up the stasis and restore circulation, often relieving the lingering discomfort and finally allowing the discoloration to clear.

faqs.question: What foods should I eat to help bruises heal?
faqs.answer: Warm, cooked foods that promote circulation are best. Think turmeric, ginger, black pepper, dark cherries, pineapple, and leafy greens. Avoid excessive cold or raw foods, which can constrict the vessels and slow healing. If you bruise easily, add Qi- and Blood-nourishing foods like bone broth, dates, and lean meats to your diet.
